Physiology 04.question: ১) Parathormone (PTH) is mainly secreted by the........ of the parathyroid glands?
Physiology 04.exp:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is secreted primarily by the chief (principal) cells of the parathyroid glands. PTH is released in response to low serum ionized calcium detected by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR). It increases serum calcium by:

  • Stimulating bone resorption (indirectly via osteoblast-mediated activation of osteoclasts).

  • Increasing renal calcium reabsorption while decreasing phosphate reabsorption.

  • Stimulating 1α-hydroxylase in the kidney, increasing calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) formation, which enhances intestinal calcium absorption.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Oxyphil cells: Function is uncertain; they produce little or no PTH.

  • Parietal cells: Found in the stomach and secrete HCl and intrinsic factor.

  • Precursor cells: Not a functional secretory cell type of the parathyroid gland.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chief (principal) cells: Secrete PTH

  • Oxyphil cells: Larger, eosinophilic; function largely unknown

  • PTH effects: ↑ Serum Ca²⁺, ↓ Serum phosphate

  • Stimulus for PTH secretion: Low ionized Ca²⁺

  • PTH inhibits: Renal phosphate reabsorption (proximal tubule)

Exam Pearl:
Remember: Chief cells make PTH; parietal cells make gastric acid—do not confuse the two.

Physiology 04.question: ২) Secretion from........ gives milky appearance to the semen?
Physiology 04.exp:
The prostate gland secretes a thin, milky, slightly acidic fluid that constitutes about 20–30% of semen. This prostatic secretion contains citrate, zinc, acid phosphatase, and proteolytic enzymes (including prostate-specific antigen, PSA), which help liquefy semen after ejaculation and enhance sperm motility. The characteristic milky appearance of semen is mainly due to this prostatic fluid.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Testes: Produce spermatozoa, not the milky fluid.

  • Seminal vesicles: Secrete a viscous, alkaline, fructose-rich yellowish fluid.

  • Bulbourethral glands: Secrete clear mucus for lubrication.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prostate gland: Milky fluid, 20–30% of semen

  • Seminal vesicles: 60–70% of semen; fructose, prostaglandins, semenogelin

  • Testes: Produce sperm

  • Bulbourethral glands: Clear lubricating mucus

  • PSA: Liquefies coagulated semen

Exam Pearl:
The milky appearance of semen is due to prostatic secretion, whereas the largest volume of semen comes from the seminal vesicles.

Physiology 04.question: ৩) Which endocrine gland acts without pituitary control?
Physiology 04.exp:
The parathyroid glands function independently of pituitary control. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion is regulated directly by the serum ionized calcium concentration through the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on chief cells. A fall in serum calcium stimulates PTH secretion, while a rise suppresses it.

The other glands are under pituitary influence:

  • Thyroid → Stimulated by TSH from the anterior pituitary.

  • Adrenal cortex → Mainly regulated by ACTH (especially the zona fasciculata and reticularis).

  • Ovary → Regulated by FSH and LH.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Parathyroid: Regulated by serum Ca²⁺, not by the pituitary.

  • Thyroid: TSH → T₃, T₄ secretion.

  • Adrenal cortex: ACTH → Cortisol secretion.

  • Ovary: FSH and LH regulate follicular development and ovulation.

  • Aldosterone secretion is mainly controlled by the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and serum K⁺, not ACTH.

Exam Pearl:
Parathyroid is the classic endocrine gland that functions independently of pituitary control; PTH secretion is governed directly by serum ionized calcium.

Physiology 04.question: ৪) Oxytocin is made up of upto ....... amino acids?
Physiology 04.exp:
Oxytocin is a nonapeptide hormone, meaning it consists of 9 amino acids. It is synthesized in the paraventricular (mainly) and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus and transported down the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract to the posterior pituitary, where it is stored and released. Oxytocin stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction during labor and milk ejection (let-down reflex) by contracting myoepithelial cells of the mammary glands.

The other options are incorrect:

  • 20 amino acids – Not oxytocin.

  • 51 amino acids – Corresponds to insulin (A chain 21 + B chain 30).

  • 98 amino acids – Not oxytocin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Oxytocin: 9 amino acids (nonapeptide)

  • ADH (vasopressin): Also a nonapeptide (9 amino acids)

  • Site of synthesis: Hypothalamus

  • Site of storage/release: Posterior pituitary

  • Actions: Uterine contraction and milk ejection

Exam Pearl:
Both oxytocin and ADH are nonapeptides (9 amino acids) synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

Physiology 04.question: ৫) Which hormone controls blood phosphate level?
Physiology 04.exp:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is the principal hormone regulating serum phosphate (and calcium) levels. PTH decreases serum phosphate by inhibiting phosphate reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules, leading to phosphaturia. Simultaneously, it increases serum calcium by enhancing renal calcium reabsorption, stimulating bone resorption (indirectly), and increasing calcitriol synthesis, which promotes intestinal calcium absorption.

The other options are incorrect:

  • ADH: Regulates water balance.

  • Aldosterone: Regulates sodium and potassium balance.

  • Thyroxine: Regulates basal metabolic rate, not phosphate homeostasis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PTH: ↑ Serum Ca²⁺, ↓ Serum phosphate

  • Kidney: ↓ Phosphate reabsorption (proximal tubule)

  • PTH: Stimulates 1α-hydroxylase → ↑ Calcitriol

  • Calcitriol: Increases intestinal absorption of both Ca²⁺ and phosphate

  • Calcitonin: Minor role in phosphate regulation

Exam Pearl:
PTH is the key hormone controlling phosphate homeostasis by increasing renal phosphate excretion while raising serum calcium.

Physiology 04.question: ৬) What is the percentage of sperm in semen?
Physiology 04.exp:
Spermatozoa account for approximately 10% of the semen volume. The remaining ~90% is contributed by the accessory sex glands:

  • Seminal vesicles: ~60–70%

  • Prostate gland: ~20–30%

  • Bulbourethral and urethral glands: Small amount (<5%)

Although sperm constitute only about 10% of the semen volume, they are the essential cellular component responsible for fertilization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sperm (testes/epididymis): ~10%

  • Seminal vesicles: 60–70% (fructose-rich, alkaline fluid)

  • Prostate gland: 20–30% (milky fluid containing PSA, citrate)

  • Bulbourethral glands: <5% (mucus for lubrication)

  • Normal semen volume: 2–5 mL

Exam Pearl:
Most of the semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles, while spermatozoa contribute only about 10% of the ejaculate.

Physiology 04.question: ৭) Which hormone causes ovulation?
Physiology 04.exp:
Ovulation is triggered by the mid-cycle surge of luteinizing hormone (LH). Rising estrogen levels from the dominant follicle exert positive feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, leading to a sharp LH surge around the middle of the menstrual cycle. This surge causes rupture of the mature (Graafian) follicle, release of the ovum, and subsequent formation of the corpus luteum.

The other options are incorrect:

  • FSH: Stimulates follicular growth and maturation.

  • Estrogen: Induces the LH surge but does not directly cause ovulation.

  • Progesterone: Secreted after ovulation by the corpus luteum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • FSH: Follicular growth

  • LH surge: Triggers ovulation

  • Estrogen: Positive feedback → LH surge

  • Progesterone: Maintains the secretory endometrium after ovulation

  • Corpus luteum: Formed after ovulation under LH influence

Exam Pearl:
Remember: FSH grows the follicle, but the LH surge releases the ovum (ovulation).

Physiology 04.question: ৮) What is single best investigation for thyroid function?
Physiology 04.exp:
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is the single best investigation for thyroid function in most clinical situations. TSH is secreted by the anterior pituitary and regulates thyroid hormone production. Because of the sensitive negative feedback relationship between thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄) and TSH, a small change in thyroid hormone levels produces a significant change in TSH concentration. Therefore, serum TSH measurement is the most sensitive screening test for detecting primary thyroid dysfunction.

The other options:

  • FT3: Less useful as a screening test; may remain normal in early hypothyroidism.

  • FT4: Helps assess severity and classify thyroid disorders but is usually interpreted with TSH.

  • Thyroid scan: Evaluates thyroid structure and function, not the initial thyroid function test.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Best initial thyroid function test: Serum TSH

  • Primary hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH, ↓ FT4

  • Primary hyperthyroidism: ↓ TSH, ↑ FT4/FT3

  • FT4: Useful for confirming and grading thyroid dysfunction

  • Thyroid scan: Used for nodules, goiter, and hyperthyroidism evaluation

Exam Pearl:
TSH is the most sensitive and first-line test for assessing thyroid function in suspected primary thyroid disease.

Physiology 04.question: ৯) Normally tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below......... ?
Physiology 04.exp:
Tetany occurs when the ionized calcium concentration decreases, increasing neuromuscular excitability. Clinically, tetany usually appears when total plasma calcium falls below approximately 8 mg/dL (normal total calcium ≈ 9–11 mg/dL). Low calcium reduces the threshold for nerve and muscle activation, leading to symptoms such as perioral tingling, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, and seizures in severe cases.

The other options are incorrect:

  • 2 mg/dL, 4 mg/dL, 6 mg/dL: Represent severe hypocalcemia levels and are not the usual threshold at which tetany begins.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Normal plasma calcium: ≈ 9–11 mg/dL

  • Tetany occurs when calcium falls below: ≈ 8 mg/dL

  • Major causes of hypocalcemic tetany:

    • Hypoparathyroidism

    • Vitamin D deficiency

    • Chronic kidney disease

  • Signs of tetany:

    • Trousseau sign

    • Chvostek sign

Exam Pearl:
Tetany usually appears when plasma calcium falls below about 8 mg/dL due to increased neuromuscular excitability.

Physiology 04.question: ১০) Maximum catecholamines are removed from body through urine in which form?
Physiology 04.option2: Free or conjugated meta-adrenaline and meta-noradrenaline
Physiology 04.exp:
The major route of catecholamine metabolism is through monoamine oxidase (MAO) and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), producing inactive metabolites. The major urinary end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline metabolism is vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), which accounts for the largest proportion of catecholamine metabolites excreted in urine. Measurement of urinary VMA has been used historically for diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Free adrenaline and noradrenaline: Only a small fraction is excreted unchanged.

  • Metanephrines (met-adrenaline and met-noradrenaline): Important metabolites and now commonly measured clinically, but not the main final urinary end product.

  • Phenylethanolamine: Not the major urinary metabolite.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adrenaline → Metanephrine → VMA

  • Noradrenaline → Normetanephrine → VMA

  • VMA: Major urinary end product of catecholamine metabolism.

  • Pheochromocytoma: Increased catecholamines and their metabolites.

Exam Pearl:
The principal urinary end product of catecholamine metabolism is vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).

Physiology 04.question: ১১) Which type of dwarfism occurs due to deficiency of somatomedin?
Physiology 04.exp:
Levi-Lorain dwarfism (also called Laron syndrome) occurs due to deficiency of somatomedin C (IGF-1) or resistance to growth hormone (GH). In this condition, GH levels are usually normal or elevated, but the liver cannot respond properly to GH, resulting in reduced IGF-1 production and impaired growth of bones and tissues.

The other options:

  • Panhypopituitary dwarfism: Due to deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones, including GH deficiency, leading to reduced IGF-1.

  • GH deficiency dwarf: Caused by low GH secretion.

  • Sexual ateliotic dwarf: Associated with delayed sexual development and genetic disorders, not specifically somatomedin deficiency.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GH → Liver → IGF-1 (Somatomedin C) → Bone/cartilage growth

  • Laron syndrome: GH receptor defect → ↓ IGF-1 → dwarfism

  • Pituitary dwarfism: ↓ GH → ↓ IGF-1

  • Laron dwarfism: ↑ GH + ↓ IGF-1

Exam Pearl:
Somatomedin (IGF-1) deficiency with normal/high GH levels causes Laron (Levi-Lorain) dwarfism.

Physiology 04.question: ১২) Which gland is called the ‘life-saving gland’?
Physiology 04.exp:
The adrenal gland is called the “life-saving gland” because its hormones, especially glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), are essential for survival. Cortisol helps maintain blood glucose, vascular tone, stress response, and metabolism, while aldosterone maintains sodium balance, extracellular fluid volume, and blood pressure. Complete loss of adrenal cortex function (as in severe adrenal insufficiency) can be fatal without hormone replacement.

The other options:

  • Thyroid: Regulates metabolism and growth but is not essential for immediate survival.

  • Parathyroid: Regulates calcium balance; severe dysfunction can cause tetany but is not called life-saving gland.

  • Pancreas: Regulates glucose metabolism through insulin and glucagon.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adrenal gland = life-saving gland

  • Adrenal cortex: Cortisol, aldosterone, and adrenal androgens

  • Adrenal medulla: Adrenaline and noradrenaline

  • Cortisol: Essential for stress response and maintaining vascular responsiveness

Exam Pearl:
Adrenal gland is called the life-saving gland because adrenal cortical hormones are essential for maintaining life.

Physiology 04.question: ১৩) What is not a cause of thyroid overactivity?
Physiology 04.exp:
Cretinism is not a cause of thyroid overactivity; it is a condition of congenital hypothyroidism due to inadequate thyroid hormone production during fetal or early childhood development. It leads to impaired physical growth and intellectual development.

The causes of thyroid overactivity (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) include:

  • Graves’ disease: Autoimmune stimulation of TSH receptors causing increased thyroid hormone production.

  • Toxic goiter: Excessive thyroid hormone production from hyperfunctioning thyroid tissue.

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: Usually causes hypothyroidism, but it may rarely cause transient hyperthyroidism (Hashitoxicosis) due to release of stored thyroid hormones.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyperthyroidism causes: Graves’ disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma

  • Cretinism: Congenital hypothyroidism

  • Graves’ disease: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism

  • Hashimoto thyroiditis: Most common cause of acquired hypothyroidism

Exam Pearl:
Cretinism is a condition of thyroid hormone deficiency, not thyroid overactivity.

Physiology 04.question: ১৪) Low sperm count with less than 20 million of sperms/mL of semen is called.....?
Physiology 04.exp:
Oligozoospermia (oligospermia) refers to a reduced sperm concentration in semen. A sperm count of less than 20 million sperm/mL of semen (traditional WHO reference value) is classified as oligozoospermia. It may contribute to male infertility due to reduced chances of fertilization.

The other options:

  • Azoospermia: Complete absence of spermatozoa in semen.

  • Aspermia: Absence of semen (failure of ejaculation or semen production).

  • Oligospermia/Oligozoospermia: Low sperm count (reduced sperm concentration).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Oligozoospermia: ↓ sperm count (<20 million/mL in older exam criteria)

  • Azoospermia: No sperm present

  • Aspermia: No ejaculate/semen

  • Asthenozoospermia: Reduced sperm motility

  • Teratozoospermia: Abnormal sperm morphology

Exam Pearl:
Low sperm count = oligozoospermia; absence of sperm = azoospermia.

Physiology 04.question: ১৫) Adrenaline increases force of contraction of heart by positive....... effect?
Physiology 04.exp:
Adrenaline (epinephrine) increases the force of contraction of the heart by producing a positive inotropic effect. It acts mainly through β₁-adrenergic receptors in cardiac muscle, increasing cAMP formation, which enhances calcium influx into cardiac myocytes and increases the strength of myocardial contraction.

The other options:

  • Chronotropic effect: Increases heart rate (positive chronotropic effect).

  • Bathmotropic effect: Increases excitability of cardiac muscle.

  • Dromotropic effect: Increases conduction velocity, especially through the AV node.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • β₁ stimulation by adrenaline:

    • ↑ Heart rate → Positive chronotropic

    • ↑ Force of contraction → Positive inotropic

    • ↑ Conduction velocity → Positive dromotropic

    • ↑ Excitability → Positive bathmotropic

  • Calcium availability is the key factor for increased cardiac contractility.

Exam Pearl:
Force of cardiac contraction = Inotropic effect; heart rate = Chronotropic effect.

Physiology 04.question: ১৬) In which condition frog like husky voice is found?
Physiology 04.exp:
A frog-like husky voice is a classic feature of myxoedema, which occurs due to severe hypothyroidism. In hypothyroidism, deposition of mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans) in tissues causes myxoedematous changes, including edema and thickening of the vocal cords, producing a deep, hoarse, husky voice. Other features include lethargy, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, and bradycardia.

The other options:

  • Cretinism: Congenital hypothyroidism causing impaired growth and intellectual disability; may have a hoarse cry/voice but the classic adult finding is myxoedema.

  • Graves’ disease: Causes hyperthyroidism, not husky voice.

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: A cause of hypothyroidism, but the clinical feature described is classically associated with myxoedema.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Myxoedema: Severe adult hypothyroidism

  • Features:

    • Hoarse/frog-like husky voice

    • Non-pitting edema

    • Weight gain

    • Cold intolerance

    • Bradycardia

  • Graves’ disease: Hyperthyroidism with exophthalmos and goiter

  • Cretinism: Childhood hypothyroidism

Exam Pearl:
Frog-like husky voice is a classic clinical feature of myxoedema due to hypothyroid-related vocal cord changes.

Physiology 04.question: ১৭) Hypersecretion of growth hormone after the union of epiphysis & diaphysis results in.......?
Physiology 04.exp:
Hypersecretion of growth hormone (GH) after the fusion of epiphysis and diaphysis causes acromegaly. After epiphyseal closure, the long bones cannot increase in length, so excess GH acts mainly on soft tissues and causes enlargement of hands, feet, jaw, facial bones, and internal organs through increased insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) production.

The other options:

  • Gigantism: Occurs when GH excess happens before epiphyseal closure, causing excessive linear growth and increased height.

  • Dwarfism: Results from GH deficiency during childhood.

  • Cretinism: Due to congenital hypothyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GH excess before epiphyseal closure → Gigantism

  • GH excess after epiphyseal closure → Acromegaly

  • GH deficiency in childhood → Pituitary dwarfism

  • IGF-1: Main mediator of GH effects on growth

Exam Pearl:
Epiphyseal closure determines the outcome of GH excess: before closure = gigantism, after closure = acromegaly.

Physiology 04.question: ১৮) Inability to perform sexual intercourse is called.....?
Physiology 04.exp:
Impotency (erectile dysfunction) refers to the inability to perform sexual intercourse, usually due to failure to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for intercourse. It is a disorder of sexual function and may result from vascular, neurological, hormonal, psychological, or drug-related causes.

The other options:

  • Sterility: Inability to produce offspring due to inability to generate viable sperm or ova.

  • Infertility: Inability to achieve pregnancy despite regular unprotected intercourse (may be due to male or female factors).

  • Castration: Removal or destruction of testes/ovaries leading to loss of gonadal function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Impotency: Failure of sexual performance/intercourse

  • Infertility: Failure to produce offspring

  • Azoospermia: Absence of sperm in semen

  • Castration: Loss of gonadal function due to removal/destruction

Exam Pearl:
Impotency = inability to perform sexual intercourse; infertility/sterility = inability to produce offspring.

Physiology 04.question: ১৯) Pheochromocytoma is a condition characterized by hypersecretion of.........?
Physiology 04.exp:
Pheochromocytoma is a tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla characterized by excessive secretion of catecholamines (mainly adrenaline and noradrenaline). These hormones produce symptoms such as episodic hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations, and tremor due to excessive sympathetic stimulation.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Glucocorticoids: Secreted by the adrenal cortex; excess causes Cushing syndrome.

  • Mineralocorticoids: Mainly aldosterone; excess causes Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism).

  • Sex corticoids: Adrenal androgens; excess may cause virilization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pheochromocytoma: Adrenal medulla tumor

  • Hormones: Catecholamines (epinephrine + norepinephrine)

  • Classic triad:

    • Headache

    • Sweating

    • Palpitations

  • Diagnosis: Measurement of plasma/urinary metanephrines

Exam Pearl:
Pheochromocytoma = “tumor of catecholamines” from adrenal medulla chromaffin cells.

Physiology 04.question: ২০) Which one is male pill?
Physiology 04.exp:
Gossypol is a compound derived from cottonseed that has been studied as a male contraceptive pill. It acts mainly by affecting spermatogenesis, causing a reduction in sperm production and motility. However, due to concerns about irreversible infertility and toxicity (especially hypokalemia), it is not widely used as a standard contraceptive method.

The other options are female contraceptives:

  • Cyclofem: Injectable combined hormonal contraceptive for females.

  • Lippes loop: An intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD).

  • Norplant: A levonorgestrel-releasing subdermal implant for females.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gossypol: Experimental male contraceptive

  • Cyclofem: Monthly injectable female contraceptive

  • Lippes loop: IUCD

  • Norplant: Progestin implant

  • Male contraceptive methods: Condoms, vasectomy, and experimental hormonal methods

Exam Pearl:
Gossypol is classically remembered as the “male pill” in reproductive physiology MCQs.

Physiology 04.question: ২১) Excessive ADH results in which of the following?
Physiology 04.exp:
Excessive secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) causes Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH). Increased ADH leads to excessive water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of the kidney through increased aquaporin-2 channel insertion, causing dilutional hyponatremia, reduced plasma osmolality, and concentrated urine.

The other options:

  • DI (Diabetes insipidus): Due to ADH deficiency or renal resistance to ADH, causing excessive dilute urine.

  • DM (Diabetes mellitus): Due to insulin deficiency or resistance.

  • HUNK: Not a recognized endocrine disorder.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ↑ ADH → SIADH

    • Hyponatremia

    • Low plasma osmolality

    • Concentrated urine

  • ↓ ADH/action → Diabetes insipidus

    • Polyuria

    • Polydipsia

    • Dilute urine

  • ADH site of action: Collecting duct (V₂ receptors)

Exam Pearl:
Excess ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia → SIADH.

Physiology 04.question: ২২) Hypothyroidism leads to......... in children?
Physiology 04.exp:
Hypothyroidism in children leads to cretinism, a condition caused by insufficient thyroid hormone during fetal life or early childhood. Thyroid hormones are essential for normal brain development, growth, and maturation of the skeleton. Deficiency results in mental retardation, short stature, delayed bone development, and characteristic physical features if untreated.

The other options:

  • Myxoedema: Severe hypothyroidism occurring mainly in adults.

  • Goiter: May occur due to thyroid enlargement from various causes, including iodine deficiency or Hashimoto thyroiditis, but is not the defining outcome of childhood hypothyroidism.

  • Exophthalmos: A feature of Graves’ disease (hyperthyroidism).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Childhood hypothyroidism → Cretinism

  • Adult hypothyroidism → Myxoedema

  • Hyperthyroidism (Graves’) → Exophthalmos

  • Thyroid hormone functions:

    • Brain development

    • Growth

    • Bone maturation

Exam Pearl:
Remember: Hypothyroidism in children causes cretinism, while hypothyroidism in adults causes myxoedema.

Physiology 04.question: ২৩) All of the hormones are necessary for spermatogenesis except.....?
Physiology 04.exp:
Progesterone is not essential for spermatogenesis. Normal sperm production requires the coordinated action of FSH, testosterone, and small amounts of estrogen. FSH acts on Sertoli cells to stimulate spermatogenesis and production of androgen-binding protein (ABP). Testosterone from Leydig cells is essential for maturation of sperm cells within the seminiferous tubules. Estrogen, produced by aromatization of testosterone, also has a supportive role in male reproductive function.

The other options:

  • FSH: Essential for Sertoli cell function and spermatogenesis.

  • Testosterone: Essential for sperm maturation.

  • Estrogen: Required in small amounts for normal male reproductive physiology.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • FSH → Sertoli cells → Spermatogenesis

  • LH → Leydig cells → Testosterone production

  • Testosterone + FSH → Normal sperm formation

  • Estrogen: Supports male reproductive function

  • Progesterone: Not a key hormone for spermatogenesis

Exam Pearl:
Spermatogenesis depends mainly on FSH and testosterone; progesterone has no essential role.

Physiology 04.question: ২৪) Which one is not a feature of hyperthyroidism?
Physiology 04.exp:
Weight gain is not a feature of hyperthyroidism. Excess thyroid hormones increase basal metabolic rate (BMR), causing increased energy expenditure and usually weight loss despite increased appetite. Hyperthyroidism is characterized by increased sympathetic activity and metabolic acceleration, producing symptoms such as nervousness/excitability, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, and muscle weakness.

The other options are features of hyperthyroidism:

  • Excitability: Due to increased sympathetic nervous system activity.

  • Muscle weakness: Common due to increased protein breakdown and thyrotoxic myopathy.

  • Heat intolerance: Due to increased metabolic heat production.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyperthyroidism:

    • ↑ BMR → Weight loss

    • Heat intolerance

    • Tachycardia

    • Nervousness/excitability

    • Muscle weakness

  • Hypothyroidism:

    • ↓ BMR → Weight gain

    • Cold intolerance

    • Bradycardia

    • Lethargy

Exam Pearl:
Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss; hypothyroidism causes weight gain.

Physiology 04.question: ২৫) Sex hormones are secreted from which part of adrenal gland?
Physiology 04.exp:
The zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex secretes adrenal sex hormones (androgens), mainly dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and androstenedione. These weak androgens contribute to the development of secondary sexual characteristics, especially in females.

The adrenal cortex follows the mnemonic “GFR”:

  • Zona Glomerulosa: Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)

  • Zona Fasciculata: Glucocorticoids (cortisol)

  • Zona Reticularis: Sex steroids (androgens)

The other options:

  • Adrenal medulla: Secretes catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • G → Salt (Glomerulosa → Aldosterone)

  • F → Sugar (Fasciculata → Cortisol)

  • R → Sex (Reticularis → Androgens)

  • Adrenal cortex hormones are mainly regulated by ACTH except aldosterone.

Exam Pearl:
Zona reticularis = adrenal androgen (sex hormone) secretion.

Physiology 04.question: ২৬) Which one has anti inflammatory effect?
Physiology 04.exp:
Cortisol is the major glucocorticoid secreted by the adrenal cortex and has a powerful anti-inflammatory effect. It reduces inflammation by inhibiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes through inhibition of phospholipase A₂ activity (via lipocortin/annexin-1). It also suppresses immune cell activity and cytokine production.

The other options:

  • Aldosterone: Mineralocorticoid; regulates sodium and potassium balance, not inflammation.

  • Androgen: Mainly involved in sexual development and anabolic effects.

  • Epinephrine: Catecholamine; increases cardiovascular responses but is not a primary anti-inflammatory hormone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cortisol = anti-inflammatory + immunosuppressive

  • Glucocorticoids inhibit:

    • Prostaglandins

    • Leukotrienes

    • Cytokine production

  • Aldosterone: Na⁺ retention, K⁺ excretion

  • Adrenal medulla: Epinephrine and norepinephrine

Exam Pearl:
Cortisol is the body’s main anti-inflammatory hormone and the basis of steroid anti-inflammatory therapy.

Physiology 04.question: ২৭) Dexamethasone suppression test is an investigation for.....?
Physiology 04.exp:
The dexamethasone suppression test is used mainly for the diagnosis and evaluation of Cushing’s syndrome (hypercortisolism). Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid that normally suppresses ACTH secretion from the pituitary through negative feedback, resulting in reduced cortisol production. In patients with Cushing’s syndrome, this suppression pattern is abnormal and helps differentiate the cause of cortisol excess.

The other options:

  • Addison's disease: Due to adrenal insufficiency; evaluated by ACTH stimulation test.

  • Addison's crisis: An acute adrenal emergency; assessed clinically with cortisol/electrolytes.

  • Conn's syndrome: Primary hyperaldosteronism; evaluated by aldosterone-renin ratio.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dexamethasone suppression test → Cushing’s syndrome

  • ACTH stimulation test (Synacthen test) → Addison’s disease

  • Cushing syndrome: ↑ Cortisol

  • Conn syndrome: ↑ Aldosterone → hypertension + hypokalemia

  • Dexamethasone does not interfere with cortisol assay.

Exam Pearl:
Dexamethasone suppression test is the classic screening test for Cushing’s syndrome.

Physiology 04.question: ২৮) Which is true for Type I DM?
Physiology 04.exp:
Type I diabetes mellitus is caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency. It usually occurs in children and young adults and has a relatively rapid onset of symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue. Patients are often lean and may present with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

The other options are incorrect:

  • Usually after 40 years: Type I DM commonly occurs before 40 years; Type II is more common later in life.

  • Lack of insulin receptor: Seen in rare insulin resistance disorders, not Type I DM.

  • Usually overweight: Typical of Type II DM due to insulin resistance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Type I DM:

    • Autoimmune β-cell destruction

    • Absolute insulin deficiency

    • Usually young age

    • Lean body habitus

    • Rapid symptom onset

    • Risk of DKA

  • Type II DM:

    • Insulin resistance

    • Usually overweight

    • Gradual onset

Exam Pearl:
Type I DM = absent insulin production + young age + rapid onset + risk of ketoacidosis.

Physiology 04.question: ২৯) Hypo secretion of adrenal cortex results in.....?
Physiology 04.exp:
Hyposecretion of the adrenal cortex causes Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency). It occurs due to inadequate production of adrenal cortical hormones, mainly cortisol and aldosterone. Common features include weakness, weight loss, hypotension, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia due to reduced cortisol and mineralocorticoid activity.

The other options:

  • Cushing's syndrome: Caused by excess cortisol secretion (adrenal cortex hyperfunction or other causes).

  • Conn's syndrome: Caused by excess aldosterone secretion (primary hyperaldosteronism).

  • Adrenal hyperplasia: Refers to enlargement of adrenal tissue, often due to increased ACTH stimulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adrenal cortex hypofunction → Addison’s disease

  • Adrenal cortex hormones:

    • Zona glomerulosa → Aldosterone

    • Zona fasciculata → Cortisol

    • Zona reticularis → Androgens

  • Addison’s disease: ↓ Cortisol + ↓ Aldosterone

  • Cushing syndrome: ↑ Cortisol

Exam Pearl:
Low adrenal cortex hormones = Addison’s disease; high cortisol = Cushing’s syndrome.

Physiology 04.question: ৩০) Which is the most abundant cell in the islets of Langerhans?
Physiology 04.exp:
The B cells (β-cells) are the most abundant cells in the islets of Langerhans, making up approximately 60–70% of the islet cell population. They are mainly located in the central portion of the islets and secrete insulin, which regulates blood glucose levels by promoting glucose uptake and storage.

The other options:

  • A cells (α-cells): Secrete glucagon; about 20–25% of islet cells.

  • D cells (δ-cells): Secrete somatostatin; about 5–10%.

  • PP cells: Secrete pancreatic polypeptide; least abundant.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • β-cells (60–70%) → Insulin

  • α-cells (20–25%) → Glucagon

  • δ-cells (5–10%) → Somatostatin

  • PP/F cells → Pancreatic polypeptide

  • Insulin is the only major hormone that lowers blood glucose.

Exam Pearl:
Beta cells are the most abundant cells of the islets of Langerhans and are responsible for insulin secretion.

Physiology 04.question: ৩১) which one is anti diabetogenic hormone?
Physiology 04.exp:
Insulin is the anti-diabetogenic hormone because it lowers blood glucose levels and prevents the development of diabetes mellitus. It promotes glucose uptake by skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, stimulates glycogenesis, and inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Glucagon: A diabetogenic hormone; increases blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

  • Cortisol: Diabetogenic; increases blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis and reducing glucose utilization.

  • Thyroxine: Can increase blood glucose by enhancing metabolism but is not the anti-diabetogenic hormone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Insulin = anti-diabetogenic hormone

    • ↓ Blood glucose

    • ↑ Glucose uptake

    • ↑ Glycogenesis

  • Diabetogenic hormones:

    • Glucagon

    • Cortisol

    • Growth hormone

    • Catecholamines

    • Thyroid hormones

Exam Pearl:
Insulin is the only major hormone that lowers blood glucose; therefore, it is called the anti-diabetogenic hormone.

Physiology 04.question: ৩২) Which factor stimulates insulin secretion?
Physiology 04.exp:
Acetylcholine (ACh) stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells. It acts mainly through muscarinic M3 receptors and increases intracellular calcium, promoting insulin release. This occurs during the cephalic and intestinal phases of digestion through parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation.

The other options:

  • Epinephrine: Inhibits insulin secretion via α₂-adrenergic receptors and increases blood glucose.

  • Norepinephrine: Also inhibits insulin release through sympathetic stimulation.

  • Somatostatin: Inhibits insulin secretion from β-cells and glucagon secretion from α-cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Stimulators of insulin secretion:

    • ↑ Blood glucose (major stimulus)

    • Amino acids

    • Incretins (GLP-1, GIP)

    • Acetylcholine

  • Inhibitors of insulin secretion:

    • Sympathetic stimulation (epinephrine, norepinephrine)

    • Somatostatin

Exam Pearl:
Parasympathetic acetylcholine stimulates insulin release, while sympathetic catecholamines inhibit it.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৩) Which hormone has permissive action?
Physiology 04.exp:
Cortisol has a classic permissive action. It does not directly produce some effects but allows other hormones to exert their full action. Cortisol increases the responsiveness of blood vessels to catecholamines by upregulating α₁-adrenergic receptors, helping maintain normal vascular tone and blood pressure. Without cortisol, the effects of catecholamines are reduced, leading to hypotension.

The other options:

  • Catecholamine: Produces direct effects such as increased heart rate and vasoconstriction but is not classically permissive.

  • Aldosterone: Regulates sodium and potassium balance; not a permissive hormone.

  • ADH: Regulates water reabsorption in kidneys; not a classic permissive hormone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cortisol permissive effects:

    • Enhances catecholamine action on cardiovascular system

    • Maintains vascular responsiveness

    • Supports gluconeogenesis

  • Examples of permissive hormones:

    • Cortisol → catecholamine action

    • Thyroid hormone → catecholamine action

Exam Pearl:
Cortisol is the classic permissive hormone that allows catecholamines to maintain normal blood pressure.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৪) Which one is an acute complication of DM?
Physiology 04.exp:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute complication of diabetes mellitus, especially Type I DM. It occurs due to severe insulin deficiency, leading to increased lipolysis, formation of ketone bodies, metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance. It is a medical emergency.

The other options are chronic complications of diabetes:

  • Retinopathy: Chronic microvascular complication affecting the retina.

  • Nephropathy: Chronic microvascular complication affecting the kidneys.

  • Stroke: A macrovascular complication due to long-term diabetic vascular damage.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acute complications of DM:

    • DKA (Type I DM)

    • Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) (Type II DM)

    • Hypoglycemia

  • Chronic complications:

    • Retinopathy

    • Nephropathy

    • Neuropathy

    • Cardiovascular disease

    • Stroke

Exam Pearl:
DKA is an acute, life-threatening complication of diabetes, mainly associated with Type I DM.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৫) Which hormone has receptor in cytoplasm?
Physiology 04.exp:
Steroid hormones have intracellular receptors, mainly located in the cytoplasm or nucleus. Being lipid-soluble, steroids can cross the cell membrane and bind to cytoplasmic receptors. The hormone–receptor complex then enters the nucleus and regulates gene transcription.

Examples of steroid hormones:

  • Cortisol

  • Aldosterone

  • Estrogen

  • Progesterone

  • Testosterone

The other options:

  • Thyroxin (T3/T4): Has nuclear receptors (not cytoplasmic receptors).

  • PTH: Peptide hormone; acts through cell membrane receptors (GPCR).

  • GH: Protein hormone; acts through cell membrane receptors (JAK-STAT pathway).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Intracellular receptors:

    • Steroid hormones → cytoplasmic/nuclear receptors

    • Thyroid hormones → nuclear receptors

    • Vitamin D → nuclear receptors

  • Membrane receptors:

    • Peptide hormones (GH, insulin, PTH)

    • Catecholamines

Exam Pearl:
Steroid hormones are classically associated with cytoplasmic receptors and regulation of gene transcription.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৬) Primary aldosteronism is called....?
Physiology 04.exp:
Primary aldosteronism is called Conn’s syndrome. It occurs due to excessive secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex, most commonly due to an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Excess aldosterone causes increased sodium and water retention, leading to hypertension, along with increased potassium and hydrogen ion loss, causing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

The other options:

  • Cushing's syndrome: Due to excess cortisol secretion.

  • Addison's disease: Due to deficiency of adrenal cortex hormones (cortisol ± aldosterone).

  • Addison's crisis: Acute severe adrenal insufficiency.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Conn’s syndrome = ↑ Aldosterone

    • Hypertension

    • Hypokalemia

    • Metabolic alkalosis

    • ↓ Plasma renin (primary form)

  • Cushing’s syndrome = ↑ Cortisol

  • Addison’s disease = ↓ Adrenal cortex hormones

Exam Pearl:
Primary hyperaldosteronism = Conn’s syndrome (excess aldosterone causing hypertension + hypokalemia).

Physiology 04.question: ৩৭) The entire period of spermatogenesis takes about...... days?
Physiology 04.exp:
The entire process of spermatogenesis takes approximately 74 days. It includes the transformation of spermatogonia → primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids → spermatozoa within the seminiferous tubules of the testes. After formation, sperm require additional time for maturation and storage in the epididymis.

The other options:

  • 36 days: Not the complete duration of spermatogenesis.

  • 48 days: Shorter than the actual process.

  • 86 days: Longer than the standard duration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spermatogenesis duration: ~74 days

  • Site: Seminiferous tubules of testes

  • FSH: Acts on Sertoli cells → supports spermatogenesis

  • LH: Acts on Leydig cells → testosterone production

  • Testosterone: Essential for sperm maturation

Exam Pearl:
Remember: Complete spermatogenesis takes about 74 days.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৮) Failure of a testes to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum is termed as.......?
Physiology 04.exp:
Cryptorchidism is the condition in which one or both testes fail to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum. Normally, testicular descent occurs during fetal life, mainly under the influence of androgens and gubernaculum development. Failure of descent can lead to infertility and increases the risk of testicular cancer.

The other options:

  • Orchitis: Inflammation of the testis, commonly due to infection (e.g., mumps).

  • Cryptitis: Inflammation of a crypt (not related to testicular descent).

  • Testicular atrophy: Shrinkage and loss of testicular tissue due to various causes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cryptorchidism = undescended testis

  • Common site of undescended testis: inguinal canal

  • Complications:

    • Infertility (due to higher abdominal temperature)

    • Increased risk of testicular malignancy

  • Normal testicular temperature: 2–3°C lower than body temperature

Exam Pearl:
Failure of testicular descent into the scrotum = Cryptorchidism.

Physiology 04.question: ৩৯) What is primary sexual organ in male?
Physiology 04.exp:
The testes are the primary sexual organs (gonads) in males because they perform the two essential reproductive functions:

  1. Production of sperm (spermatogenesis)

  2. Secretion of male sex hormone (testosterone) by Leydig cells

The other options:

  • Penis: Accessory external genital organ involved in copulation and semen delivery.

  • Scrotum: A sac that protects and maintains the testes at a lower temperature for sperm production.

  • Epididymis: Site of sperm maturation and storage, but not a primary sexual organ.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Male primary sexual organ → Testes

    • Sertoli cells → Support spermatogenesis, secrete inhibin

    • Leydig cells → Produce testosterone

  • Female primary sexual organs → Ovaries

    • Produce ova and female sex hormones

Exam Pearl:
Gonads are primary sexual organs: testes in males and ovaries in females.

Physiology 04.question: ৪০) the period of fertility in female during each month is about...... days?
Physiology 04.exp:
The fertile period in females during each menstrual cycle is about 4–5 days. This period includes the time around ovulation, when fertilization is most likely to occur. Although the ovum remains viable for about 24 hours after ovulation, sperm can survive in the female reproductive tract for approximately 3–5 days, making the fertile window longer.

The other options:

  • 1–2 days: Too short; represents mainly the lifespan of the ovum after ovulation.

  • 2–3 days: Does not include the full sperm survival period.

  • 3–4 days: Close but shorter than the commonly accepted fertile period.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ovulation: Usually occurs around 14th day in a 28-day cycle.

  • Ovum survival: ~24 hours.

  • Sperm survival in female tract: ~3–5 days.

  • Fertile period: Approximately 4–5 days around ovulation.

Exam Pearl:
Female fertile period ≈ 4–5 days because sperm survive longer than the ovum.

Physiology 04.question: ৪১) Type-1 DM occurs due to actual deficiency of which hormone?
Physiology 04.exp:
Type-1 diabetes mellitus (DM) occurs due to an absolute deficiency of insulin caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells in the islets of Langerhans. Lack of insulin leads to decreased glucose uptake by cells and increased blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia). Patients are at risk of developing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) due to increased fat breakdown and ketone body formation.

The other options:

  • ADH: Deficiency causes diabetes insipidus, not diabetes mellitus.

  • Glucagon: Excess increases blood glucose; it is not deficient in Type-1 DM.

  • Cortisol: Excess can cause hyperglycemia (Cushing syndrome).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Type-1 DM:

    • ↓ Insulin production

    • β-cell destruction

    • Usually young age

    • Lean body habitus

    • Risk of DKA

  • Type-2 DM:

    • Insulin resistance

    • Relative insulin deficiency

Exam Pearl:
Type-1 DM = absolute insulin deficiency due to pancreatic β-cell destruction.

Physiology 04.question: ৪২) Which is the commonest cell group in anterior pituitary?
Physiology 04.exp:
The somatotroph cells are the most common cell group in the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis), comprising about 40–50% of anterior pituitary cells. They secrete growth hormone (GH), which promotes body growth through IGF-1 (somatomedin C) production from the liver.

The other options:

  • Corticotroph: Secretes ACTH; about 15–20% of anterior pituitary cells.

  • Thyrotroph: Secretes TSH; about 5%.

  • Mammotroph (Lactotroph): Secretes prolactin; about 10–20%.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Somatotroph → GH → Most abundant anterior pituitary cell

  • Mammotroph → Prolactin

  • Corticotroph → ACTH

  • Thyrotroph → TSH

  • Gonadotroph → FSH & LH

Exam Pearl:
Anterior pituitary’s most abundant cell = Somatotroph (GH-secreting cell).

Physiology 04.question: ৪৩) Mineralocorticoids are transported in blood by binding with which plasma protein?
Physiology 04.exp:
Mineralocorticoids (mainly aldosterone) are transported in the blood by binding mainly to plasma proteins, especially corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG/transcortin) and albumin. Among the given options, globulin is the best answer because steroid hormones are commonly transported bound to specific globulin proteins.

The other options:

  • Albumin: Also binds some steroid hormones due to its high plasma concentration.

  • Transferrin: Transports iron, not steroid hormones.

  • Trans protein: Not a standard plasma transport protein for mineralocorticoids.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid): Mostly bound to plasma proteins; small amount free.

  • Cortisol: Mainly bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG/transcortin).

  • Thyroid hormones: Bound mainly to thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG).

  • Steroid hormones: Lipid-soluble → require carrier proteins in blood.

Exam Pearl:
Mineralocorticoids are transported in blood mainly by globulin (especially corticosteroid-binding globulin).

Physiology 04.question: ৪৪) Which hormone is related to satiety control?
Physiology 04.exp:
Leptin is the hormone primarily involved in satiety control (appetite suppression). It is secreted by adipose tissue and acts on the hypothalamus to decrease food intake and increase energy expenditure. Higher fat stores → increased leptin secretion → reduced appetite under normal conditions.

The other options:

  • Adiponectin: Secreted by adipocytes; improves insulin sensitivity and fatty acid metabolism, but not the main satiety hormone.

  • Relaxin: A reproductive hormone involved in pregnancy and parturition.

  • Thymin: Not a major hormone involved in appetite regulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Leptin → Satiety signal ("I am full")

  • Ghrelin → Hunger signal ("I am hungry")

  • Leptin source: Adipocytes

  • Leptin action: Hypothalamus → ↓ appetite

Exam Pearl:
Leptin is the key adipose-derived hormone responsible for satiety control.

Physiology 04.question: ৪৫) The beta-chain of insulin contains how many amino acids?
Physiology 04.exp:
Human insulin is composed of two polypeptide chains:

  • A-chain: 21 amino acids

  • B-chain: 30 amino acids

These two chains are linked by disulfide bonds to form active insulin. The complete insulin molecule contains a total of 51 amino acids.

The other options:

  • 21: Number of amino acids in the A-chain of insulin.

  • 51: Total amino acids in both A + B chains.

  • 91: Not related to insulin structure.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Insulin structure:

    • A-chain → 21 amino acids

    • B-chain → 30 amino acids

    • Total → 51 amino acids

  • Produced by β-cells of islets of Langerhans

  • Insulin decreases blood glucose level.

Exam Pearl:
Insulin B-chain = 30 amino acids; total insulin molecule = 51 amino acids.

Physiology 04.question: ৪৬) PP cells of pancreas secretes........?
Physiology 04.exp:
PP cells (gamma cells/F cells) of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans secrete pancreatic polypeptide (PP). Pancreatic polypeptide helps regulate exocrine pancreatic secretion, gastrointestinal motility, and appetite-related functions.

The other options:

  • Insulin: Secreted by β (beta) cells.

  • Glucagon: Secreted by α (alpha) cells.

  • Somatostatin: Secreted by δ (delta) cells.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Pancreatic islet cell Hormone
β-cell Insulin
α-cell Glucagon
δ-cell Somatostatin
PP/F-cell Pancreatic polypeptide

Exam Pearl:
PP cells → Pancreatic polypeptide (remember: PP = Pancreatic Polypeptide).

Physiology 04.question: ৪৭) Which one has longest half life?
Physiology 04.exp:
Thyroxin (T4) has the longest half-life among the given hormones. The half-life of T4 is approximately 7 days because it is highly bound to plasma proteins, mainly thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), which slows its clearance from the blood.

The other options:

  • PTH: Very short half-life (~2–5 minutes) due to rapid degradation.

  • Insulin: Half-life is about 5 minutes.

  • Glucagon: Half-life is about 5–10 minutes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • T4 (Thyroxine): Half-life ≈ 7 days (longest)

  • T3: Half-life ≈ 1 day

  • Insulin: ~5 minutes

  • PTH: ~2–5 minutes

  • Glucagon: ~5–10 minutes

Exam Pearl:
Among thyroid and pancreatic hormones, thyroxine (T4) has the longest half-life.

Physiology 04.question: ৪৮) Which one is the most active adrenal androgen?
Physiology 04.exp:
Testosterone is the most active androgen among the given options. Although the adrenal cortex secretes mainly weak androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and androstenedione from the zona reticularis, these can be converted in peripheral tissues to more potent androgens, especially testosterone.

The other options:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA): Major adrenal androgen secretion but has weak androgenic activity.

  • Androstenedione: Weak androgen; precursor of testosterone.

  • Cortisol: A glucocorticoid, not an androgen.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Zona reticularis → adrenal androgens

    • DHEA (major adrenal androgen)

    • Androstenedione

  • Most potent naturally occurring androgen → Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)

  • Most active androgen among given options → Testosterone

Exam Pearl:
Adrenal cortex produces weak androgens (DHEA, androstenedione), while testosterone is the active androgen.

Physiology 04.question: ৪৯) What is the chemical nature of the hormone Thyroxine?
Physiology 04.exp:
Thyroxine (T4) is a tyrosine derivative hormone. It is synthesized in the thyroid gland from the amino acid tyrosine by iodination of thyroglobulin. Thyroxine contains four iodine atoms, hence it is also called tetraiodothyronine (T4).

The other options:

  • Steroid: Steroid hormones are derived from cholesterol (e.g., cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones).

  • Alcohol: Not a hormone chemical class.

  • Protein: Peptide/protein hormones include insulin, GH, and PTH.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tyrosine-derived hormones:

    • Thyroxine (T4)

    • Triiodothyronine (T3)

    • Catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline)

  • Steroid hormones: Derived from cholesterol

    • Cortisol

    • Aldosterone

    • Testosterone

  • Peptide hormones:

    • Insulin

    • GH

    • PTH

Exam Pearl:
Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) are iodinated tyrosine derivatives.

Physiology 04.question: ৫০) Which hormone stimulates milk ejection from alveoli into ducts?
Physiology 04.exp:
Oxytocin stimulates milk ejection (let-down reflex) from the alveoli of the mammary gland into the ducts during breastfeeding. It causes contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, pushing milk into the lactiferous ducts for delivery.

The other options:

  • Prolactin: Stimulates milk production (lactogenesis) by mammary gland alveolar cells, not milk ejection.

  • Relaxin: Involved in pregnancy changes and pelvic ligament relaxation.

  • Inhibin: Regulates FSH secretion and reproductive function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prolactin → Production of milk

  • Oxytocin → Ejection of milk (let-down reflex)

  • Oxytocin source: Posterior pituitary

  • Prolactin source: Anterior pituitary

Exam Pearl:
Remember: Prolactin makes milk, oxytocin moves milk.
